title: Proxy for OpenAI Codex and Claude Code, use any LLM with those apps
author: dandaka
summary: This item describes the concept of a "proxy" that allows you to use various large language models (LLMs) with applications originally built to work with specific models, like OpenAI Codex or Claude. Think of a proxy as an intermediary. Instead of your application talking directly to, say, OpenAI's API, it talks to your proxy. The proxy then translates your application's requests and sends them to whichever LLM you configure it to use, and then sends the LLM's response back to your application. This offers great flexibility, letting you experiment with different models, potentially use self-hosted LLMs, or switch providers without rewriting your entire application. It's a practical approach for building more adaptable and future-proof generative AI systems.
why: Enables flexible LLM integration, crucial for adaptable GenAI applications.

title: Show HN: We stopped feature-gating our open source BI platform
author: nikhelical
raw_text:
Hi HN, Nikhilesh here — c0founder of Helical Insight.We've been building Helical Insight for few years now as an open source BI platform, used for interactive dashboards, pixel-perfect/paginated reporting, embedded analytics, and now AI-powered conversational analytics.Today we've made a major change to our open source strategy.Instead of keeping advanced capabilities behind an Enterprise Edition, we've made the Community Edition feature-complete. It now includes AI analytics (bring your own LLM), embedding, SSO, multi-tenancy, row-level security, white labeling, scheduling, report bursting, dashboards, and pixel-perfect reporting. Source code present on Github.The only differences are:Community Edition includes a small "Helical Insight" branding on charts and exports that cannot be removed.
Community support is provided through our forum, while Enterprise customers receive SLA-backed support and can remove the branding.Our reasoning is simple: developers and organizations should be able to evaluate and use the complete platform instead of an artificially limited edition. We'd rather build our business around support, services, and enterprise SLAs than around feature gating.The project is primarily Java-based & react based, supports self-hosting, Docker, Kubernetes, and integration with multiple databases and identity providers. For AI, we lately introduced Python also.I'd genuinely appreciate feedback from anyone using Superset, Metabase, Redash, Lightdash, JasperReports, Pentaho, Crystal Reports, or SSRS.What would stop you from adopting an open source BI platform today? Happy to answer any technical or architectural questions.
summary: This news highlights a shift in strategy for an open-source business intelligence (BI) platform, Helical Insight, which has made its advanced features, including AI analytics, available in its free community edition. This is significant because it shows a trend towards democratizing powerful AI capabilities, allowing more developers and organizations to integrate AI into their data analysis and reporting tools without needing an expensive enterprise license. For you, this means more opportunities to work with AI-powered analytics, potentially using your own LLMs, in real-world BI contexts. It also illustrates how AI is being integrated into various software domains, expanding the scope of AI engineering. You could explore open-source BI platforms that now offer AI features to understand their architecture and potential for customization.
why: Shows AI integration in BI, democratizing advanced features for broader use.

title: NetBSD GSoC 2026 Reports: Testing Compat Linux: Syscall Testing
author: jaypatelani
summary: This news item discusses a Google Summer of Code (GSoC) project for NetBSD, which is an open-source operating system. The project focuses on "syscall testing" within NetBSD's Linux compatibility layer. Essentially, it's about making sure that programs designed for Linux can run correctly on NetBSD by accurately replicating how Linux system calls behave. While this is a foundational aspect of operating system development and ensures software compatibility, it's quite low-level and not directly related to your core interests in AI, data science, or large language models. However, understanding how different systems ensure compatibility can sometimes offer broader insights into robust software engineering practices.
why: Less relevant to AI/DS, but highlights general software compatibility testing.

title: Two-Level Meta-Rubrics for Evaluating Open-Ended Generation: GAMUT, a Benchmark for Factual Completeness
author: Xilun Chen, Zhaleh Feizollahi, Ross Goodwin, Seungwhan Moon, Scott Yih, Pinar Donmez, Babak Damavandi, Luna Dong
raw_text: Evaluating the factuality of long-form generations has focused predominantly on precision, measuring whether the claims a model makes are correct. The dominant decompose-search-verify pipeline catches incorrect claims well but says little about whether a response contains all the information it should. Measuring factual completeness, the missing half of factuality, is harder: it requires enumerating the full set of facts a complete answer should contain, and these facts rarely form a flat list. They often involve open-ended sets where coverage is what matters, ordered processes, and relationships among facts that a list of independent boolean checks fails to capture. We introduce a two-level meta-rubric framework for evaluating open-ended generation, and instantiate it as Gamut (Grounded Assessment of Multimodal Factuality), a benchmark for factual completeness in long-form generation. The framework rests on a two-level rubric representation: a structured meta-rubric captures the organization and importance of the required content, which is then mechanically compiled into a flat checklist of binary, machine-gradable rubrics that an LLM judge scores reliably. We construct 1,813 questions grounded in real wearable imagery across 10 diverse domains, each paired with an evidence-backed rubric verified by expert human annotators. Because the framework is modality-agnostic, we also release a text-only variant. Evaluating 14 frontier and open-weight models, we find the benchmark genuinely challenging (best score 58.7% from Gemini 3.1 Pro), highly discriminative, and robust to the choice of judge.
summary: When evaluating large language models (LLMs), we often focus on whether their generated text contains incorrect information, which is called factual precision. However, this paper introduces an important concept: factual completeness. It means checking if an LLM's response includes all the necessary information it should, not just that the information it *does* provide is correct. Imagine asking an LLM about a topic; if it only gives you a few correct facts but misses many other crucial ones, its answer isn't truly complete. This is harder to measure because a complete answer isn't just a simple list of facts. The paper presents GAMUT, a benchmark to help evaluate this missing half of factuality. Understanding this distinction is vital for building robust and trustworthy generative AI systems.
why: Crucial for building reliable RAG/GenAI; evaluates if LLMs give complete answers.

title: In-House LLM Serving at Netflix
author: sbulaev
summary: This news highlights that Netflix is building its own infrastructure to serve large language models (LLMs) internally. Instead of relying solely on external LLM providers, they are developing custom solutions to deploy, manage, and scale these models within their own systems. This approach allows for greater control over data, performance optimization, and cost efficiency for various applications across their platform, from content recommendations to internal tools. For you, this demonstrates the real-world engineering challenges and sophisticated MLOps practices involved in bringing advanced AI models into production at a large scale. It's a key aspect of making AI practical and sustainable within an organization.
why: Shows real-world LLM deployment challenges and MLOps solutions at scale.

title: AutoSynthesis: An agentic system for automated meta-analysis
author: Moein Taherinezhad, Sebastian Maier, Gerardo Vitagliano, Francesco Pierri, Stefan Feuerriegel
raw_text: Evidence synthesis is crucial for turning primary research into reliable knowledge for science, medicine, education, and policy. Yet, quantitative evidence synthesis remains largely manual and difficult to scale. Here, we introduce AutoSynthesis, an end-to-end multi-agent system for automated meta-analysis. Given a research question in natural language, AutoSynthesis formulates a search strategy, retrieves scientific literature, screens candidate studies, assesses full-text eligibility, extracts quantitative statistics, computes standardized effect sizes, and finally performs random-effects meta-analysis. AutoSynthesis further supports heterogeneity analysis to examine how effect sizes vary across moderators, as well as risk-of-bias assessment. As output, AutoSynthesis produces a transparent report aligned with PRISMA guidelines. In our application, AutoSynthesis screened over 28 studies and extracted more than 20 quantitative claims. The pooled effect estimates produced by AutoSynthesis are similar to Hedges' $g$ of expert-conducted meta-analyses, indicating close agreement with manual evidence synthesis. Together, these results show that AutoSynthesis can make quantitative evidence synthesis more scalable, thereby supporting evidence-based decision-making across disciplines.
summary: this paper introduces autosynthesis, a multi-agent system designed to automate meta-analysis, which is the process of combining results from multiple studies to draw stronger conclusions. traditionally, this is a very manual and time-consuming task. autosynthesis uses different ai agents, each specialized for a step like formulating search queries, retrieving literature, screening studies, and extracting data. this showcases how agents can collaborate to tackle complex, multi-step problems, which is a key area in ai. understanding how these agents are designed to work together can give you insights into building robust ai systems that can automate complex workflows, especially in research and development.
why: shows how multi-agent systems automate complex research tasks, a key agent application.
